subject: OpenAI's revenue run rate is $50B, not $70B
bodyMarkdown:
Most people reading this own a slice of the AI trade without ever choosing it, through an index fund in a TFSA or a workplace pension. Last week that trade wobbled on a single revenue number, and the number turned out to be something investors had built themselves.

## The $70 billion was arithmetic, not a disclosure

The Financial Times reported on Thursday that OpenAI's **annualized revenue**, meaning the latest month of sales multiplied out to a full year, sat near $50 billion at the end of September. Investors had been working off $70 billion. The gap came from how that figure got assembled. OpenAI counts its core sales and leaves out revenue booked through third-party cloud channels, while Anthropic includes them, so analysts grossed OpenAI's number up to compare the two and landed near $40 billion for August. Then OpenAI told investors revenue had grown 70 per cent, and that growth went on top of the already inflated base. That is where $70 billion came from. The reporting does not say demand fell or growth stalled. It says the market spent weeks quoting its own estimate back to itself.

## One bad Thursday, and then everyone moved on

The reaction was fast and then it was finished. CNBC reported that the Nasdaq fell about 1.25 per cent on Thursday to 27,193 as the AI trade stumbled on the revenue story, with the S&P 500 off 0.47 per cent, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down 3.4 per cent, Oracle lower by more than 5 per cent, and Nvidia and AMD each off roughly 3 to 4 per cent. By Friday it had all come back. The Washington Post's Friday scoreboard put the S&P 500 up 0.59 per cent at 7,811.51, the Dow up 0.83 per cent at 51,655.01 and the Nasdaq up 0.64 per cent at 27,366.17, leaving the S&P 1.2 per cent higher on the week and a few points under the 7,844.52 record it reached earlier in the week. Cheaper oil helped, with Brent sliding from $104.28 after Trump said on Thursday that the United States would not strike Iran before the November 3 midterms.

## That number is collateral now

Here is the part that bothers me. OpenAI is private, so there are no audited statements to check against, and the figures in circulation come from investor updates and leaks. I wrote on Friday about Broadcom arranging more than $50 billion of **private credit**, which is lending by investment firms instead of banks, to fund OpenAI's custom chips, with Apollo and Blackstone among the firms reported to be in talks. Bloomberg pegged the next phase closer to $30 billion. Either way, lenders are sizing multi-year debt against a revenue picture the market had wrong by $20 billion last month. Equity can absorb a repricing in an afternoon, which is roughly what Friday was. Debt schedules cannot. And the chip and cloud companies that dropped on Thursday are the ones whose order books assume OpenAI keeps paying.

## The takeaway

Third-quarter earnings start this week, so I would listen to what Oracle and Microsoft say about how they recognize AI revenue, not just what they say about demand. Ask for the method behind any AI revenue figure you see quoted, because the $70 billion version lasted weeks before a reporter went and checked it. If you hold a broad American index fund, look up how much of it sits in the handful of names that fell on Thursday, because that is your real exposure. Yahoo Finance's wrap noted the 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.36 per cent last week, the highest since 2002, and debt-funded compute gets harder to justify at that price.
